title: Wēn el-mahatta — asking the way
goal: Ask for directions and actually understand the answer, use commands, and say where things are in relation to each other.
bekal: ask where a place is with three different patterns
understand the commands رُوح، لِف، اِمْشِي and their feminine forms
give directions and locations with the right preposition

dialogs.title: حَكِي — عَ الطَّرِيق
dialogs.intro: Budi is lost looking for a bus stop in Amman and asks a man standing outside a shop.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Excuse me, where's the bus stop?

lines.speaker: اَلرِّجَّال:
lines.text: أَهْلًا. قَرِيبِة، تْقَرِيبًا خَمْس دَقَايِق مَشِي.
lines.id: Hello. It's close, about five minutes' walk.
lines.literal: family. near, roughly five minutes walking.

lines.speaker: اَلرِّجَّال:
lines.id: Walk straight to the end of the street.

lines.speaker: اَلرِّجَّال:
lines.text: اِمْشِي شْوَي كَمَان، بْتْشُوف بَنْك عَ الشِّمَال.
lines.baca: imshi shway kamaan, btshuuf bank ‘a esh-shimaal.
lines.id: Walk a bit more and you'll see a bank on the left.
lines.literal: walk a-little also, you-see bank on the-left.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: And the stop is in front of the bank?

lines.speaker: اَلرِّجَّال:
lines.id: No, behind the bank. Next to the mosque.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: فْهِمِت. وْأَيّ بَاص بْيَاخُدْنِي عَ وَسَط الْبَلَد؟
lines.baca: fhimt. w ayy baaṣ byaakhudni ‘a wasaṭ el-balad?
lines.id: Got it. And which bus goes downtown?
lines.literal: I-understood. and which bus it-takes-me on center the-town?

lines.speaker: اَلرِّجَّال:
lines.text: رَقَم سِتَّة. بَسّ اِسْأَل السَّوَّاق لَتْأَكَّد.
lines.baca: ra’m sitte. bass is’al es-sawwaa’ lat’akkad.
lines.id: Number six. But ask the driver to make sure.
lines.literal: number six. but ask the-driver to-you-make-sure.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Thanks a lot. God keep you.

lines.speaker: اَلرِّجَّال:
lines.baca: wala yhimmak. ahlan w sahlan fiik.
lines.id: No problem at all. You're welcome.
lines.literal: and-not it-troubles-you. family and ease in-you.

notes: **Commands are made by dropping the prefix from the "you" form.** بْتِمْشِي ("you walk") becomes اِمْشِي ("walk!"). For a woman add ـِي — اِمْشِي stays اِمْشِي, but رُوح becomes رُوحِي and لِف becomes لِفِّي.

**The word دُغْرِي means "straight," and it isn't originally Arabic.** It comes from Turkish, a leftover of four centuries of Ottoman rule, and is used all over the Levant. You'll hear it in every set of directions.
**Right and left take the preposition عَ.** The forms are عَ الْيَمِين and عَ الشِّمَال. In parts of Lebanon and Palestine, "left" is عَ الْيَسَار — both are correct and understood everywhere.

**The word عِنْد means "at" for landmarks, not just "have."** عِنْد الصَّيْدَلِيِّة means "at the pharmacy" as a reference point, exactly like "at the lights" or "by the church" in English directions.

**The phrase وْلَا يْهِمَّك is the most typically Levantine reply to thanks.** Literally "may it not trouble you," it means "no problem at all." It's much warmer than عَفْوًا, and using it instantly makes you sound like less of a tourist.

**Don't be shy about asking twice.** Directions come fast and are often long. Your lifesavers: مُمْكِن تْعِيد؟ ("could you repeat?") and شْوَي شْوَي لَو سَمَحْت ("slowly, please"). Both are polite and always work.

grammars.title: Commands
after: To forbid, put لَا before the **ordinary verb without b-**, not before the command form: لَا تْرُوح ("don't go"), لَا تِسْأَل ("don't ask"). لَا رُوح is wrong and sounds off right away.
⚠️ Bare commands sound blunter in English than in Arabic. تَعَال to a friend is perfectly normal. But to someone older or a stranger, add لَو سَمَحْت, or turn it into a question: مُمْكِن تِيجِي؟

rows: between the bank and the shop

after: These words also take the possessive endings from unit 4: قِدَّامِي ("in front of me"), وَرَايِ ("behind me"), جَنْبَك ("next to you"). These forms are very common for saying where something is relative to you.
The words فَوْق and تَحِت are also used for floors of a building: الطَّابِق فَوْق ("upstairs"), تَحِت ("downstairs"). In tall buildings, floors are given with ordinary numbers: اَلطَّابِق التَّالِت.

blocks.text: The word حَمَّام does double duty: it means the bathroom at home and the public restroom anywhere else. وَين الْحَمَّام؟ is always understood and isn't considered rude anywhere in the Levant.

blocks.title: Three ways to ask, and how they differ
items: For location: وَين + place + ؟ — وَين الْبَنْك؟ The most direct.
For how to get there: كِيف بُوصَل عَ…؟ — كِيف بُوصَل عَ الْمَطَار؟ The answer is a set of directions.
For whether it exists: فِي + place + هُون؟ — فِي صَيْدَلِيِّة قَرِيبِة؟ The answer is simply yes or no.

blocks.text: The word سِرْفِيس refers to a shared van that runs a fixed route and stops anywhere along it. It's much cheaper than a taxi, and riding one is the fastest way to feel you really live in the city.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Taxis and meters
items: In Amman and Beirut, ask for عَ الْعَدَّاد ("by the meter") before you get in. If the driver refuses, agree on the price first: قَدِّيش لَـ…؟
Agreeing on a price before you set off isn't a sign of distrust — it's simply what everyone does.
To get out, say وَقِّف هُون لَو سَمَحْت or, more typically, عَ جَنْب ("pull over a moment").
Excuse me, where's the bus stop?
Walk straight to the end of the street.
The stop is behind the bank.
How do I get to the airport?
